content: But now he has obtained a more excellent ministry, by as much as he is also the mediator of a better covenant, which on better promises has been given as law. {{v:7}} For if that first covenant had been faultless, then no place would have been sought for a second. {{v:8}} For finding fault with them, he said, “Behold, the days are coming”, says the Lord, “that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah; {{v:9}} not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers in the day that I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt; for they didn’t continue in my covenant, and I disregarded them,” says the Lord. {{v:10}} “For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days,” says the Lord: “I will put my laws into their mind; I will also write them on their heart. I will be their God, and they will be my people. {{v:11}} They will not teach every man his fellow citizen and every man his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord,’ for all will know me, from their least to their greatest. {{v:12}} For I will be merciful to their unrighteousness. I will remember their sins and lawless deeds no more.” {{v:13}} In that he says, “A new covenant”, he has made the first obsolete. But that which is becoming obsolete and grows aged is near to vanishing away.

facets.text: Christ's priestly ministry surpasses the Levitical order precisely in proportion to the covenant he mediates: because his covenant rests on better promises, his mediation is correspondingly more excellent. The passage grounds the superiority of Christ's priesthood not merely in his person but in the quality of the covenant he inaugurates. Mediation and covenant are inseparable here—the greatness of the one measures the greatness of the other.
facets.question: Why is Christ's priestly ministry greater than that of the old priesthood?

facets.text: The very promise of a 'new covenant' spoken through Jeremiah reveals that the first covenant was not final. The author reasons that if the first arrangement had been faultless, no second would have been sought; thus God's own word anticipated its replacement. Scripture itself testifies to the provisional character of the Mosaic economy.
facets.question: How does the Old Testament itself point beyond the old covenant to a new one?

facets.text: The fault of the first covenant lay not in God's law but in the people who did not remain faithful to it—'they didn't continue in my covenant.' The remedy of the new covenant is therefore interior: God will write his laws upon the mind and heart rather than only on tablets of stone. This transposition from external command to inward grace anticipates the gift of the Holy Spirit who conforms the believer's will to God from within.
facets.question: Why does the new covenant write God's law on the heart instead of on stone?

facets.text: The new covenant renews the ancient covenant formula, 'I will be their God, and they will be my people,' now realized in a deeper communion. Where the old bond was mediated through teachers and external instruction, the new promises that 'all will know me, from their least to their greatest.' This universal, direct knowledge of God foreshadows the intimacy of grace and, ultimately, the beatific vision.
facets.question: What does it mean that everyone will know God directly under the new covenant?

facets.text: At the heart of the new covenant stands the promise of forgiveness: 'I will remember their sins and lawless deeds no more.' Unlike the repeated sacrifices of the old law that recalled sin year after year, the new covenant offers a definitive mercy grounded in Christ's once-for-all offering. This forgiveness is the foundation on which the interior law and the knowledge of God become possible.
facets.question: How does the new covenant deal with sin differently than the old?

facets.text: By calling the covenant 'new,' God has declared the first 'obsolete,' aged, and near to vanishing away. The author does not despise the old covenant but reads its passing as part of God's providential unfolding of salvation history. What was a genuine but preparatory dispensation yields to its fulfillment in Christ, so that the old finds its true meaning in what it foreshadowed.
facets.question: Why does the coming of the new covenant make the old one obsolete?

merged.annotation:
SUMMARY: Hebrews 8:6–13 presents Christ as mediator of a better covenant founded on better promises, citing Jeremiah's prophecy of a new covenant with interior law, universal knowledge of God, definitive forgiveness, and the resulting obsolescence of the first covenant.

[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: Christ's priestly ministry is more excellent because it mediates a better covenant on better promises; mediation and covenant are proportionate.
[SCRIPTURAL | explicit]: The prophesied new covenant proves the first was not final—had it been faultless, no second would have been sought.
[DOCTRINAL | traditional]: The old covenant's fault lay in the unfaithful people; the new writes God's law on mind and heart, anticipating the Spirit's interior grace.
[SCRIPTURAL | traditional]: The covenant formula 'I will be their God' is renewed as direct knowledge of God by all, foreshadowing grace and the beatific vision.
[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: Central to the new covenant is definitive forgiveness—God remembers sin no more—grounded in Christ's once-for-all offering versus repeated sacrifices.
[TYPOLOGICAL | explicit]: Declaring the covenant 'new' renders the first obsolete and near vanishing; the preparatory old dispensation yields to its fulfillment in Christ.

content: A man of God came to Eli and said to him, “The LORD says, ‘Did I reveal myself to the house of your father when they were in Egypt in bondage to Pharaoh’s house? {{v:28}} Didn’t I choose him out of all the tribes of Israel to be my priest, to go up to my altar, to burn incense, to wear an ephod before me? Didn’t I give to the house of your father all the offerings of the children of Israel made by fire? {{v:29}} Why do you kick at my sacrifice and at my offering, which I have commanded in my habitation, and honor your sons above me, to make yourselves fat with the best of all the offerings of Israel my people?’ {{v:30}} “Therefore the LORD, the God of Israel, says, ‘I said indeed that your house and the house of your father should walk before me forever.’ But now the LORD says, ‘Far be it from me; for those who honor me I will honor, and those who despise me will be cursed. {{v:31}} Behold, the days come that I will cut off your arm and the arm of your father’s house, that there will not be an old man in your house. {{v:32}} You will see the affliction of my habitation, in all the wealth which I will give Israel. There shall not be an old man in your house forever. {{v:33}} The man of yours whom I don’t cut off from my altar will consume your eyes and grieve your heart. All the increase of your house will die in the flower of their age. {{v:34}} This will be the sign to you that will come on your two sons, on Hophni and Phinehas: in one day they will both die. {{v:35}} I will raise up a faithful priest for myself who will do according to that which is in my heart and in my mind. I will build him a sure house. He will walk before my anointed forever. {{v:36}} It will happen that everyone who is left in your house will come and bow down to him for a piece of silver and a loaf of bread, and will say, “Please put me into one of the priests’ offices, that I may eat a morsel of bread.”’”

facets.text: The prophecy against Eli rests on the priesthood as sheer gift: God freely revealed himself to the house of Aaron in Egypt, chose it out of all Israel for altar and incense and ephod, and granted it the fire offerings. Because the office was received, not earned, its abuse is a betrayal of grace rather than the loss of a possession. The recital of past favor makes the coming judgment a matter of ingratitude answered.
facets.question: Why does God recount his past gifts to the priestly house before pronouncing judgment on it?

facets.text: Eli's central sin is naming: he honored his sons above God, letting them grow fat on the best of Israel's offerings and grow contempt for the sacrifice God commanded. To prefer one's own family to God's honor is to invert the order of love, treating what is holy as a means to appetite. The passage exposes how priestly privilege becomes corruption when reverence for God yields to indulgence of kin.
facets.question: What was Eli's sin in honoring his sons above God?

facets.text: God states a governing principle of his dealings: "those who honor me I will honor, and those who despise me will be cursed." This reciprocity is not arbitrary favoritism but the moral logic of covenant, where honor given to God draws honor in return and contempt reaps its own curse. It reframes the whole oracle as an instance of a universal divine justice.
facets.question: Does God honor those who honor him and reject those who despise him?

facets.text: The promise that Eli's house should "walk before me forever" is not simply revoked but transferred: God says "far be it from me" to sustaining the unfaithful line, yet raises up a faithful priest with a sure house who will walk before the anointed forever. Even an everlasting promise presupposes fidelity, and God's word advances by pruning the unworthy branch rather than abandoning his purpose. The permanence belongs to God's plan, not to any dynasty that presumes upon it.
facets.question: Can a covenant promise described as 'forever' be taken away from an unfaithful house?

facets.text: The oracle of a "faithful priest" who does according to God's heart and mind, with a sure house walking before God's anointed forever, points beyond Zadok and the immediate succession to its fulfillment in Christ, the true and eternal High Priest. The tradition reads this permanent priesthood before the Messiah-king as anticipating the one who unites priesthood and everlasting fidelity. Human priestly failure sets the stage for the priesthood that cannot fail.
facets.question: How does the promise of a faithful priest with a sure house point toward Christ?

facets.text: God gives a verifiable sign—the death of Hophni and Phinehas in a single day—so that the word may be recognized as truly his when it comes to pass. Prophecy carries its own credentials: the fulfilled sign authenticates the larger judgment and confirms that history unfolds under God's declared word. This anchors the whole oracle in the reliability of divine speech.
facets.question: Why does God give the death of Eli's sons in one day as a sign?

facets.text: The judgment reaches beyond Eli to the humiliation of his surviving descendants, who will beg for a place among the priests for a morsel of bread. The corruption that fed itself fat on the best offerings ends in men pleading for scraps, the very hunger they exploited turned back upon them. The reversal reveals that despising God's holy things hollows out the honor and security they were meant to secure.
facets.question: What becomes of a corrupt priestly line under God's judgment?

merged.annotation:
SUMMARY: A man of God pronounces God's oracle against Eli, recalling the free gift of the Aaronic priesthood, condemning Eli for honoring his corrupt sons above God, and announcing the fall of his house and the raising up of a faithful priest with an everlasting sure house before God's anointed.

[DOCTRINAL | traditional]: The priesthood is presented as unmerited gift—revealed in Egypt, chosen from all Israel, granted altar, incense, and offerings—so its abuse is betrayal of grace.
[MORAL | explicit]: Eli's sin is honoring his sons above God, letting them grow fat on the best offerings while despising the sacrifice God commanded, inverting the order of love.
[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: God declares the covenant principle that those who honor him he honors and those who despise him are cursed—the moral logic of divine justice.
[DOCTRINAL | inferential]: A promise of walking before God 'forever' is transferred rather than abandoned; permanence belongs to God's plan and presupposes fidelity, not to a presumptuous dynasty.
[TYPOLOGICAL | traditional]: The faithful priest with a sure house who walks before the anointed forever points beyond Zadok to Christ, the eternal High Priest who unites priesthood and fidelity.
[SCRIPTURAL | explicit]: The death of Hophni and Phinehas in one day is given as a sign authenticating the prophecy, showing history under God's reliable word.
[MORAL | explicit]: Eli's surviving line is reduced to begging for bread and a priestly place, the reversal of those who fed themselves fat on holy offerings.
